summary: Defines how Sieve, the email filtering language, can plug into points in IMAP where messages are created or changed. In the base specification Sieve only runs at mail delivery, so this adds the option of user-defined or interesting handling at other events. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: A mail sorter usually works only when mail arrives. This memo lets it also act when messages are saved or changed in your mailbox.

subtitle: Lets Sieve mail filters run when IMAP messages are added or flagged, not only when mail is delivered.

tldr.problem: Sieve filters normally run only at initial mail delivery, but clients that connect rarely, over slow links, or on limited devices could benefit from server-side filtering at other times too.
tldr.mechanism: A server that advertises the imapsieve capability runs a Sieve script whenever a message is created by IMAP APPEND or COPY, or has its flags changed. The script is chosen through the /shared/imapsieve/script metadata entry, and new environment items tell it what happened.
tldr.outcome: Scripts can react to the cause of the event, but delivery-only actions such as reject and vacation are errors, and implementations must prevent script loops. It updates RFC 5228.

today: RFC 6785 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2012. It updates RFC 5228, and the metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Filter Outside Delivery
sections.content:
Sieve is an email filtering language that can, in principle, plug into any point in the processing of a message. The base specification, RFC 5228, plugs it into mail delivery. RFC 6785 defines how it can also plug into points in IMAP where messages are created or changed.

The motivation is clients that are sporadically connected, use a high-latency or high-cost channel, or run on a limited-function device. For them, using server capabilities such as Sieve filtering (and extensions such as notifications) can improve performance and reliability.

Because future Sieve extensions must now say how they interact with this one, the document updates RFC 5228.
sections.eli5: Some phones and computers are slow or often offline. It helps if the mail server does the sorting work for them, not just when mail first comes in.

sections.title: How Events Differ From Delivery
sections.content:
Outside delivery, the envelope information may not be available. For a message added with IMAP APPEND there may be no way to guess the intended recipient, and no concept of who sent it, so actions that contact the sender do not apply.

User actions also work in bulk. One drag-and-drop can start script processing on a large number of messages at once, so implementations must cope with a COPY or flag change on dozens, or even thousands, of messages. Each affected message triggers its own script run, and the runs MAY be in parallel.
sections.eli5: When a letter arrives you know who sent it. When you drop a letter into a folder yourself, there is no sender to reply to, and you might drop a whole pile at once.

sections.title: Which IMAP Events Run a Script
sections.content:
A server advertises support with the IMAPSIEVE= capability, followed by the address of the ManageSieve server that clients use to manage scripts. Only one such capability string may be present. Scripts that depend on these events MUST list imapsieve in their require list. Servers MUST also support IMAP Metadata (RFC 5464) and Sieve Environment (RFC 5183).

Three kinds of event MUST trigger a script, subject to the metadata settings:

  • APPEND: a message added with the IMAP APPEND command. With MULTIAPPEND each message is a separate event.
  • COPY: messages added with the IMAP COPY command.
  • Flag changes: from FETCH, STORE or a script using imap4flags actions. The script sees the flags as they are after the change.

To avoid loops, flag changes made by a script that was itself invoked by a flag change SHOULD NOT invoke the script again, and implementations MUST take steps to avoid such loops.
sections.eli5: The sorter wakes up in three cases: a new message is saved into a folder, a message is copied there, or a message gets a flag like starred or read.

sections.title: Attaching a Script to a Mailbox
sections.content:
Scripts are attached through IMAP metadata. On an event, the server looks for a metadata entry named /shared/imapsieve/script on the mailbox. If there is none, it uses the same-named entry for the whole server, which gives a global script. If neither exists, no script runs.

The selection happens before the entry is examined. If the mailbox entry is chosen and then turns out to be empty or unusable, the server entry is not used as a backup and no script runs. The value is the name of a script on the ManageSieve server (RFC 5804); if that name does not exist, no script runs. Implementations MUST support ManageSieve and can use PUTSCRIPT without SETACTIVE.

Only one script may be defined per mailbox for now. The script itself must check the event type and ignore events it does not care about.
sections.eli5: Each folder can have a sticky note naming the one sorting recipe to use. If a folder has no note, the server-wide note is used instead.

sections.title: What Sieve Actions Mean Here
sections.content:
Because IMAP messages are immutable, any change a script makes to a message is transient and MUST NOT be kept by keep, explicit or implicit. The implicit keep means the message is treated as if no script had run.

  • fileinto creates a new message in the target mailbox, in addition to the original. It does not count as an APPEND or COPY, so it triggers no further event.
  • redirect sends the message on. If envelope data is missing, it uses message submission (RFC 6409) and the MAIL FROM SHOULD be the mailbox owner's address.
  • discard marks the original \Deleted unless an explicit keep is in effect. A script setting \Deleted does not invoke a flag-change script, and the server MAY expunge only that message.
  • notify sends the notification and handles the message as usual.

The actions reject, ereject and vacation are inapplicable. Naming them in require or using them MUST produce an error that terminates the script. Future extensions MUST specify how their actions apply.
sections.eli5: Messages in a mailbox cannot be edited, so edits only apply to copies that get sent elsewhere. Replying to a sender with an auto-reply makes no sense here, so it is not allowed.

sections.title: Environment Items
sections.content:
Scripts learn why they were invoked through the Sieve Environment extension. Two standard items change: location is set to MS (a message store) and phase is set to post.

Implementations MUST also provide new items:

  • imap.user: the login ID of the IMAP user who caused the action.
  • imap.email: that user's primary email address.
  • imap.cause: one of APPEND, COPY or FLAG.
  • imap.mailbox: the mailbox the message is in, or will be stored into. It is fixed when the script begins.
  • imap.changedflags: the flags that changed, or an empty string. It does not say whether a flag was set or cleared; the hasflag test gives the current state.

Envelope tests MUST NOT be permitted in these cases, and using one MUST generate a runtime error.
sections.eli5: The script gets a little info card saying who did something, which folder, and whether it was a save, a copy or a flag change.

sections.title: Example Scripts
sections.content:
The RFC gives two scripts. The first copies any message appended or copied into the ActionItems mailbox to actionitems@example.com using redirect :copy. The second sends a notification when the \Flagged flag is both set and part of the change, so a message that already had the flag does not notify again.

It also shows a CAPABILITY response containing IMAPSIEVE=sieve://sieve.example.com.
sections.eli5: One recipe says to forward a copy of anything saved in the Action Items folder. Another sends a ping when you star a message.

sections.title: Loops and Surprising Side Effects
sections.content:
Scripts triggered by flag changes can loop if they use imap4flags actions to change flags. Implementations MUST prevent loops. The fileinto action never triggers a script, because otherwise two mailboxes that each file into the other could loop forever. Loops are also possible through redirect and notify, and the RFC points to the advice in the base Sieve and Notify specifications.

The extension also adds side effects that users may not expect. A script could send messages marked for deletion to an off-site archive, so a user who appends an unencrypted draft and marks it for deletion might be surprised to see it sent out. Script authors need to be careful, especially with global scripts.
sections.eli5: If two folders keep sending things to each other, the mail would bounce back and forth forever, so that is blocked. Also, a simple click might send a private note somewhere, so recipe writers must be careful.
